recipe: Use size_of and align_of for compile-time layout checks, or size_of_val and align_of_val for runtime checks of a specific value's size and alignment.
trigger_condition: You need to know the size or alignment of a type or value while writing or debugging code.
evidence: Types where all values have the same size and alignment, and both are known at compile time, implement the Sized trait and can be checked with the size_of and align_of functions.

recipe: Remember that usize and isize are platform-dependent: they are 4 bytes on 32-bit targets and 8 bytes on 64-bit targets, so avoid hardcoding their size when writing portable code.
trigger_condition: You are writing code that must run on both 32-bit and 64-bit platforms and you are using usize or isize for memory calculations.
evidence: usize and isize have a size big enough to contain every address on the target platform. For example, on a 32 bit target, this is 4 bytes, and on a 64 bit target, this is 8 bytes.

recipe: Do not assume primitive alignment equals size: it is platform-specific and may be less. i128/u128 can be aligned below 16 bytes, and many 32-bit targets align i64/u64/f64 to only 4 bytes.
trigger_condition: You are computing memory layout or packing data involving 128-bit integers or 64-bit types on a potentially 32-bit target.
evidence: The alignment of primitives is platform-specific. In most cases, their alignment is equal to their size, but it may be less. In particular, i128 and u128 are often aligned to 4 or 8 bytes even though their size is 16, and on many 32-bit platforms, i64, u64, and f64 are only aligned to 4 bytes, not 8.
_original_recipe: Do not assume primitive alignment equals primitive size; i128/u128 are often aligned to only 4 or 8 bytes despite being 16 bytes, and on 32-bit platforms i64/u64/f64 may be aligned to only 4 bytes.
_review_reason: 'often 4 or 8' is stale for x86-64 (16 since Rust 1.77); keep the may-be-less rule

recipe: When working with pointers to sized types, you can treat their size and alignment as identical to usize, simplifying FFI and memory calculations.
trigger_condition: You are computing the layout of a struct containing pointers to sized types or writing FFI code.
evidence: Pointers to sized types have the same size and alignment as usize.

recipe: When computing array memory, remember that [T; N] occupies size_of::<T>() * N bytes and the nth element is at offset n * size_of::<T>() from the array start.
trigger_condition: You are manually computing memory offsets or writing FFI code involving arrays.
evidence: An array of [T; N] has a size of size_of::<T>() * N and the same alignment of T. Arrays are laid out so that the zero-based nth element of the array is offset from the start of the array by n * size_of::<T>() bytes.

recipe: The unit tuple () is a zero-sized type with size 0 and alignment 1, so it can be used as a ZST without adding any bytes to a struct.
trigger_condition: You are designing a struct or enum and want to add a tuple field without increasing the type's size.
evidence: The exception to this is the unit tuple (()), which is guaranteed as a zero-sized type to have a size of 0 and an alignment of 1.

recipe: Do not rely on the layout of closures; they have no layout guarantees, so avoid using them in FFI or when you need predictable memory layout.
trigger_condition: You are considering using a closure in a context where memory layout matters (FFI, unsafe code, or layout-sensitive data structures).
evidence: Closures have no layout guarantees.

recipe: Use the #[repr(...)] attribute to explicitly control the memory layout of your structs, enums, or unions when you need a specific arrangement.
trigger_condition: You need a specific memory layout for a composite type, such as for FFI or when you need predictable field offsets.
evidence: The representation of a type can be changed by applying the repr attribute to it.
_note: generic filler ('use repr to control layout'); specific repr rows cover it

recipe: Use #[repr(packed(N))] to lower alignment or #[repr(..., align(N))] to raise alignment when you need to control the exact alignment of a type.
trigger_condition: The default or chosen representation gives you an alignment that is too loose or too tight for your use case.
evidence: The alignment may be raised or lowered with the align and packed modifiers respectively. They alter the representation specified in the attribute. If no representation is specified, the default one is altered.

recipe: Do not apply #[repr(C)] to a zero-variant enum; it is a compile-time error. Use it only on structs, unions, or non-empty enums.
trigger_condition: You are adding #[repr(C)] to an enum and it has no variants (e.g., enum Empty {}), or you are writing FFI code with enums.
evidence: This representation can be applied to structs, unions, and enums. The exception is zero-variant enums for which the C representation is an error.

recipe: When using #[repr(C)] on a struct, the struct's alignment equals the alignment of its most-aligned field (or 1 if there are no fields), so plan your field ordering accordingly.
trigger_condition: You are defining a #[repr(C)] struct and need to predict its overall alignment for FFI or memory packing.
evidence: The alignment of the struct is the alignment of the most-aligned field in it, or one if there are no fields.

recipe: When changing a type's representation, know that it only affects padding between fields, not the internal layout of the fields themselves, so nested types keep their own representation.
trigger_condition: You are changing the repr of a struct that contains nested structs or enums and need to predict the final layout.
evidence: The representation of a type can change the padding between fields, but does not change the layout of the fields themselves.

recipe: The representation of a type is independent of its generic parameters, so Foo<Bar> and Foo<Baz> always have the same layout regardless of the type arguments.
trigger_condition: You are writing generic code and need to know whether the layout of a generic type changes with different type arguments.
evidence: the representation does not depend on generic parameters. Any two types with the same name have the same representation.
_note: wrong: repr attribute is independent of generics, but Foo<u8> and Foo<u64> obviously differ in layout
_review_reason: wrong: repr attribute is independent of generics, but Foo<u8> and Foo<u64> obviously differ in layout

recipe: When using #[repr(C)] unions, remember that all fields live at byte offset 0, the union's size is the maximum field size rounded up to its alignment, and its alignment is the maximum field alignment.
trigger_condition: You are defining a #[repr(C)] union and need to predict or verify its memory layout.
evidence: The union will have a size of the maximum size of all of its fields rounded to its alignment, and an alignment of the maximum alignment of all of its fields. These maximums may come from different fields. Each field lives at byte offset 0 from the beginning of the union.

recipe: Only apply primitive representations (e.g., #[repr(u8)]) to enumerations, never to zero-variant enums, and never combine two primitive representations on the same type.
trigger_condition: You are choosing a primitive representation for an enum.
evidence: Primitive representations can only be applied to enumerations and have different behavior whether the enum has fields or no fields. It is an error for zero-variant enums to have a primitive representation. Combining two primitive representations together is an error.

recipe: When using a primitive representation on a field-less enum, the enum's size and alignment will match the primitive type, limiting your discriminant range accordingly.
trigger_condition: You are applying a primitive representation to a field-less enum.
evidence: For field-less enums, primitive representations set the size and alignment to be the same as the primitive type of the same name. For example, a field-less enum with a u8 representation can only have discriminants between 0 and 255 inclusive.

recipe: When combining #[repr(C)] with a primitive representation (e.g., #[repr(C, u8)]), the discriminant enum will use the primitive type's size and alignment instead of the C representation.
trigger_condition: You need a smaller discriminant for a #[repr(C)] enum with fields.
evidence: For enums with fields, it is also possible to combine repr(C) and a primitive representation (e.g., repr(C, u8)). This modifies the repr(C) by changing the representation of the discriminant enum to the chosen primitive instead.

recipe: When using #[repr(align(x))], note that if x is less than the type's natural alignment, the alignment remains unchanged.
trigger_condition: You are applying an align modifier to a type.
evidence: For align, if the specified alignment is less than the alignment of the type without the align modifier, then the alignment is unaffected.

recipe: When a field is unaligned due to an alignment modifier, avoid taking a direct reference to it (undefined behavior); instead copy the value or use unaligned read/write methods.
trigger_condition: You need to access a field that is unaligned due to #[repr(packed)] or similar.

recipe: Do not apply both align and packed to the same type, and a packed type cannot transitively contain another aligned type; these modifiers only work with Rust and C representations.
trigger_condition: You are deciding which alignment modifiers to apply to a type.
evidence: The align and packed modifiers cannot be applied on the same type and a packed type cannot transitively contain another aligned type. align and packed may only be applied to the Rust and C representations.

recipe: The alignment value in #[repr(align(x))] or #[repr(packed(x))] must be a power of two between 1 and 2^29.
trigger_condition: You are specifying an alignment value for a type.
evidence: The alignment is specified as an integer parameter in the form of #[repr(align(x))] or #[repr(packed(x))]. The alignment value must be a power of two from 1 up to 229.

recipe: The transparent representation can only be used on a struct or enum with a single variant containing any number of size-0 alignment-1 fields plus at most one other field.
trigger_condition: You are deciding whether to use #[repr(transparent)] on a type.
evidence:
The transparent representation can only be used on a struct or an enum with a single variant that has:

any number of fields with size 0 and alignment 1 (e.g. PhantomData<T>), and

at most one other field.

recipe: Use #[repr(transparent)] instead of #[repr(C)] when you need a struct's ABI to match its single field's ABI, such as when interfacing with C code that expects a primitive type.
trigger_condition: You have a struct with a single primitive field and need its ABI to match that field rather than a C struct layout.
evidence: a struct with the transparent representation with a primitive field will have the ABI of the primitive field

recipe: Do not combine #[repr(transparent)] with any other representation attribute, as it delegates type layout to another type and is exclusive.
trigger_condition: You are choosing a representation attribute for a struct or enum.
evidence: it cannot be used with any other representation
